How I decide

## Taste proposes. Evidence decides.

I don't ship a decision on taste alone. For each product I pick the simplest evidence that could prove me wrong, and it is a different one every time.

- Safe Site Detector Reclame AQUI’s tool that tells people whether an online store is safe to buy from. Liking the screen wasn’t the point, understanding it was, so I tested comprehension: each person saw one version and judged a safe site. The refined version was read correctly by 74% of people, against 29%, and became V2.

- Genial App The app families use to follow their child's autism therapy. With a few hundred families, an A/B test would have been slow to teach us anything, so I tracked weekly usage and marked each release on the curve.

- LIAM An AI assistant that drafts the clinical record from the therapist's narration. With about 80 therapists, I tested the first version with them directly, and what it showed was that the drafts had to be readable. After launch, a question inside the flow tells us whether they still trust the suggestions.

- Pick & Pack The platform store, distribution-centre and delivery teams use to fulfil Fast Shop's two-hour orders. You can't split traffic in a warehouse, so one store went first and we compared it with the stores still on the old process.

About

I started in enterprise support, moved into front-end development, and found in design the work I wanted to do for life. I began with interface, then went deeper into usability to understand the people using it. From there I moved into product, to understand how those screens earn their place in the business at the end of the month and which number they move. Two postgraduate specialisations later, the path has been more and more metrics, strategy and business.

I have been the first or only designer more often than not: first Senior Product Designer at Genial Care, later leading design across two teams; sole designer for four products at Kruzer; now at Reclame Aqui, a consumer-trust platform more than 30 million people visit every month.

I'm an AI enthusiast and I work with LLMs and agents every day: to think decisions through, run research and data analysis faster, build functional prototypes, and ship some of them to production. Claude and Claude Code are where I go deepest (this site was built with them), I have worked with GPT and Gemini too, and I test new models and tools as they launch.

Case study · Healthcare · Product Growth

# Turning a forgotten app into the tool 62% of families open every day

The Genial Care family app went from an 8% daily-active rate to 62% in a year by fixing a scheduling bottleneck that was overloading operations, then letting usage decide what came next.

Role
Senior Product Designer

Team
PM · Ops lead · Eng squad · Clinical

Company
Genial Care

Timeline
2022 – 2024

Outcome
8% → 62% DAU

The short version

**Problem:** A content app almost nobody opened, on top of an operations team building every family's weekly schedule by hand.

**What I did:** Found the real bottleneck in scheduling, shipped a one-month MVP that let families see and cancel sessions, then ran a continuous loop of small bets read against a weekly behaviour curve.

**Outcome:** Daily active families went from **8.59% to 62.3%** in 13 months, in a staircase that tracks releases rather than one redesign spike.

Product strategy 0→1 Consumer healthcare Growth

In this case 6 min read

- Why it was hard

- Decision: scope the MVP

- Decision: skip the A/B test

- What shipped

- Impact

- What I’d do differently

I joined Genial Care, an ABA therapy platform for autism care, as its first Senior Product Designer, brought in to build the Atípico design system from scratch, improve the family-facing app, and stand up the clinical panel therapists use to run sessions (the same panel LIAM would later live inside). This case is about the app half of that mandate.

**01** · Why it was hard

## The bottleneck wasn't the app. It was scheduling.

**Good content, almost no opens.** The app was full of good material about autism care and almost nobody opened it. Underneath, the actual work (building every family’s weekly therapy schedule, dozens of therapists and time slots) was happening by hand. Nothing was centralised; every reschedule was a phone call.

**Growth was capped by operations capacity.** Every hour the operations team spent rescheduling by phone was an hour not spent onboarding the next family. Daily use was the metric everyone watched. Operations capacity was the actual ceiling.

**No safe base to A/B test.** Genial Care served families in the hundreds, not millions: too small to split traffic without each experiment costing weeks it didn’t have.

**02** · Decision: scope the MVP

## Scope the MVP around two actions, not a redesign

### Give families a reason to act, not just read

**Problem:** A full redesign was the obvious ask. Defending three weeks of mapping the operations team’s week (with nothing visible shipping) was hard.

**Decision:** I scoped the first release around exactly two actions: showing each child’s upcoming sessions, and letting a family cancel one themselves instead of calling. Shipped in one month, discovery to build.

**Why:** Those two actions were driving most of the manual back-and-forth between families and operations. Nobody opens a healthcare app to read about autism: they open it to find out what happens with their child on Thursday.

**What won the argument:** A map of the operations team’s week. Once the team could see the hours a single reschedule cost, nobody wanted to talk about the content grid anymore.

**Result:** Families used it immediately, and cancellations started arriving through the app instead of by phone within a few months. Proved the actual lever: give families a reason to act, not just read.

**03** · Decision: skip the A/B test

## Read behaviour against a weekly curve, not an A/B test

### The funnel said what changed. Interviews said why.

**Problem:** The textbook answer is to split traffic and A/B test each release.

**Decision:** I didn’t. Every release became its own before/after against a weekly funnel-and-curve instead: who came in, what they opened, where they stopped.

**Why:** At this scale, splitting the base in half doubles the wait for a result that already needs weeks. That's not worth it on a product whose whole advantage was learning fast.

**What it caught:** What the interviews kept returning to was rescheduling. Booking and rebooking was hard, calendars kept falling out of sync, and sometimes a therapist travelled to a session a parent had tried to cancel at the last minute, because the cancellation never reached them in time. That made cancelling a scheduling-sync problem first.

**Result:** The funnel showed which releases moved daily use; the interviews explained why. Families came back for the schedule, and every release after the MVP was chosen against that.

**04** · What shipped

## What shipped, once the mechanism was proven

Each addition earned its place the same way: does this give someone a reason to come back, measured before the next bet started.

### Sessions + cancel: the MVP

[Image: Genial Care app home screen with upcoming sessions, and session detail showing therapists and the child's evolution note]

The result of that first MVP: upcoming sessions and a therapist's note on the home screen, with cancellation now handled in-app instead of by phone.

### The PEI, translated

Sessions answer “what happened this week.” They don’t answer “is my child actually progressing?” The PEI, the individualized education plan, already existed as a clinical document families couldn’t see. I brought it into the app as a plain-language list of skills in progress, each with a start date. Not a new capability: an existing document moved to where a family could see their child inside it.

[Image: Genial Care app, PEI screen showing the child's individualized plan and the specific skills being worked on in sessions]

The PEI, translated from clinical document into something a parent can read: concrete skills, in plain language, with dates. Illustrative data.

### Genial Junto: support between sessions

The hardest moments don’t happen during a session. They happen at 8pm on a Tuesday when a child bites someone and a parent has no idea what to do. Genial Junto opened a chat run by the therapists themselves for exactly that.

The decision I’d defend here: a visible response-time badge. An open-ended “we’ll get back to you” invites obsessive checking and erodes trust. Stating “up to 2 business days” up front sets the expectation once, honestly, and lets the parent put the phone down.

[Image: Genial Junto support request flow and a conversation with a Genial advisor about a challenging behavior situation]

Genial Junto: support for the moments between sessions, with the response-time expectation stated before the parent writes anything.

**05** · Impact
Each addition shipped narrow, then was measured before the next one started. The weekly active-user chart below is the honest version of that story, release markers and all: it is a staircase with visible dips, where each step up follows a release.

8.59%
weekly average daily active users

[Image: Weekly average daily-active-user chart for the Genial Care app, rising from 8.59% in June 2023 to 62.3% in July 2024, with release markers along the timeline]

Weekly average share of families opening the app on a given day, Jun 2023 → Jul 2024: 8.59% to 62.3%. Star markers are releases: the growth tracks them, which is the point.

8.59%
Families opening the app on a given day, June 2023 baseline

62.3%
Families opening the app on a given day, July 2024, weekly average

1 month
Discovery, prototype and build for the first release

**How it was measured:** the share of families on the platform opening the app on a given day, tracked in Metabase and read as a weekly average across the 13 months from the June 2023 baseline to July 2024. The chart above is the raw weekly series (its axis labels are in Portuguese: Semana is week, Meta is the target line). Two things it does not show, stated on purpose. The first is that the base moved underneath the rate: around 30 families when I joined, around 500 when I left. The share climbed while the denominator grew roughly sixteen times, which makes the rise harder to achieve, not easier, but it does mean the 8.59% baseline sits on a much smaller base than the 62.3%. The second is that the operations-hours saving, the other pointer, was never instrumented; the operations lead s recollection is that rescheduling work went from about six hours to one, and I present it as that. One guardrail we agreed before launch: a cancellation rate above roughly 10% would have meant the change made things worse. I don’t have the closed-out reading.

**06** · What I’d do differently

## Act on the evidence sooner

I spent longer than I should have trying to make the content section work before accepting that content was not the problem. The evidence for that was available weeks before I acted on it.

Different project, different instrument. How I chose the instrument on each project →

## What came next

Once families were opening the app daily, the constraint moved to the other side of the platform: the therapists. Their bottleneck was documentation: up to two hours after every session, reconstructing what happened from memory for mandatory clinical reports. That became the next project, LIAM.

### LIAM: AI clinical documentation

An assistant that lets therapists narrate a session out loud as it happens, then drafts the required report fields for review. Session documentation went from up to 2 hours to about 25 minutes, as reported by the clinical team after rollout.

Read the case →

## Questions this page doesn't answer?

The interview findings, the features that didn't work, the guardrail numbers and how I argued against the redesign everyone wanted: all of it is a 30-minute call away.

Case study · Healthcare · AI Design

# LIAM: turning up to 2 hours of clinical paperwork into a 25-minute review

Therapists at Genial Care were losing up to two hours after every session reconstructing it from memory for mandatory clinical reports. LIAM lets them narrate instead, and hands back a draft they review and sign.

Role
Senior Product Designer

Team
PM · AI eng squad · Clinical

Company
Genial Care

Timeline
2023 – 2024

Outcome
Up to 2h → 25min per session

The short version

**Problem:** Therapists were losing up to two hours after every session reconstructing clinical records from memory, at the end of a full day.

**What I did:** Designed an AI assistant that lives inside the session screen: the therapist narrates, LIAM drafts, and the clinician reviews and signs. Most of the design time went into the failure states.

**Outcome:** Documentation went from **up to 2 hours to a 25-minute review** per session, as reported by the clinical team a quarter after rollout, with an in-product feedback loop so quality drift shows up in usage instead of months later.

AI product design Human-in-the-loop Healthcare Trust & safety

In this case 7 min read

- Why it was hard

- Decision: LIAM proposes, the clinician decides

- Decision: how I read trust

- What shipped

- Impact

- What I’d do differently

[Image: LIAM running on a tablet: the intervention screen a therapist works in during a session]

LIAM lives inside the screen therapists already use during a session, on the tablet they already have in their hand. Screens show illustrative data.

Every session at Genial Care generates a clinical record: what was targeted, what the child did, what changed. Therapists were writing that record from memory, after the fact, on top of a full day of sessions, which is exactly the kind of task that gets rushed, delayed, or thinned out under pressure. LIAM's job was to move the record-keeping into the moment it actually happens, instead of the moment there's finally time for it.

**01** · Why it was hard

## Two hours of reconstruction, and the constraint underneath it

The paperwork happened at the wrong time. A therapist finishes a session, moves to the next child, and writes the record hours later from memory, losing the specific detail from minute twelve that the record exists to capture, on top of a full day of sessions.

The number worth moving was documentation time per session, because of what sits on the other side of it: a therapist’s day has a fixed number of hours, and every hour spent reconstructing a session is an hour not spent in one. That caps how many sessions a therapist can carry, which caps how fast the company can grow the care it delivers. So documentation load limits capacity. It is also a retention risk, since unpaid evening paperwork wears clinicians down over time.

An AI feature in a clinical context fails on governance long before it fails on usability. Before I designed a screen, the team had to agree who signs the record, what the clinical record needed to contain, and how long a session recording is retained. Faster notes that said less would have moved the metric and damaged the product, so the clinical lead held a veto: a time saving bought with thinner records counted as a failure, not a win.

**02** · Decision: LIAM proposes, the clinician decides

### LIAM proposes. The clinician decides.

**Problem:** If LIAM drafts and submits on its own, authorship blurs, and a wrong clinical record with no clear author is a liability, not a convenience.

**Decision:** LIAM drafts every required field as a suggestion. A therapist reads, corrects, and submits. Nothing reaches the record unread.

**Why:** The real design question was what happens the first time it’s confidently wrong. That produced four interface rules: every field is a suggestion copied in by hand, never pre-submitted; the source recording stays attached so a therapist can check a line against what was actually said; nothing reaches the record without a person reading it; and an in-flow prompt asks whether the suggestions are still good, so quality drift shows up as a falling answer rate instead of a habit that quietly dies.

**What it caught:** Before touching the recording flow, we mapped the existing clinical panel section by section on a wall, to argue concretely about where a voice note belongs inside a workspace therapists already use, instead of assuming it needed a place of its own.

**Result:** The interaction model held through launch: LIAM proposes, the clinician decides, and record quality stayed the clinical lead’s to veto.

[Image: A wall covered in paper notes mapping the existing clinical panel: every section of the therapist's workspace laid out so the team could decide where a voice note belongs inside it]

Mapping the clinical panel as it existed, section by section, so we could argue about where an audio note belongs inside a workspace therapists already use, instead of assuming it needed a new place of its own. Photo from the project.

**03** · Decision: how I read trust

### Put the trust signal inside the flow

**Problem:** On the family app, behavior showed up in a weekly funnel. Here the population is the ~80 therapists on staff, the event happens a handful of times a day, and the real risk (a therapist quietly losing trust in a draft) never shows up in a funnel at all.

**Decision:** Put a lightweight prompt in the flow itself, asking whether LIAM’s suggestions are still good, so suggestion quality could be read from real usage after launch.

**Why:** What a therapist needs from an AI here is to keep what just happened while it’s still accurate. That made trust the thing actually at risk, more than writing quality, and a funnel can’t see a therapist who quietly stops trusting a draft but keeps clicking.

**What it caught:** Therapists tested the first version and the response was positive, with one consistent problem: LIAM transcribed the narration literally, so some passages read as fragments that didn’t make sense in a clinical record. We added a step that restructures the narration into cohesive sentences that fit the context of the session before it reaches the form, so therapists stopped rewriting the wording by hand.

**Result:** The prompt shipped with LIAM. I left Genial Care before there was a quarter of data to read, so I don’t claim what it showed.

**04** · What shipped

## What shipped

Three pieces carried the two decisions above into a working product.

### Recording, inside the work already happening

The intervention screen, with its programs, targets, and progress per skill, is where a therapist already spends the session. A single mic control sits in the corner of that exact screen, not in a separate “documentation” tool. Only the therapist is recorded: they narrate what they are doing and how the child responds. The child is never the input. Once recorded, the note surfaces as a waveform with an explicit send action, so the therapist can confirm the capture before moving on. And when an upload fails (clinics have bad wifi), the interface says so directly, “your voice note wasn’t sent,” with an obvious retry, instead of a spinner that quietly gives up.

[Image: LIAM intervention screen with progress-tracking targets and an idle voice-recording control in the corner]

The intervention screen the therapist is already working in: recording starts from a single control here.

### The draft: a form the therapist edits, not writes

This is what the two hours collapse into. LIAM turns the audio into a first draft of every required field (health check-in, reinforcers used, challenges observed, session summary, clinical discussion points) each pre-filled and clearly marked as a suggestion, with a one-click copy into the real field. The therapist’s job changes from writing the report to editing one: read, correct what’s off, keep what’s right, submit. Nothing submits itself; the “Save” action stays with the therapist.

[Image: LIAM session note form with each field pre-filled with an AI-drafted suggestion and a copy action]

The session-note form: every field carries a LIAM-drafted suggestion the therapist reviews and copies in, never submitted on their behalf.

### A feedback loop that keeps trust visible

An AI feature that quietly gets worse, or quietly gets better, teaches people to stop trusting it either way. A lightweight prompt sits directly in the flow: are you happy with LIAM’s suggestions right now, yes or no, with room to say why, so drift in suggestion quality surfaces from real usage instead of a support ticket or a churned habit months later. The decision underneath all three pieces is the same: an AI feature earns trust through visible mechanics.

[Image: LIAM feedback modal asking whether the therapist likes the suggestions LIAM is generating, with a comment field]

A direct feedback loop on the suggestions themselves: the mechanism that lets LIAM's output quality stay visible instead of assumed.

**05** · Impact

## Impact

Up to 2h
Writing the record from memory after a full day, per session, before LIAM (self-reported)

~25min
Reviewing and submitting LIAM's draft, per session, after

~80
Therapists on the clinical team: the before-and-after covers all of them, not a sample

**How it was measured, and what the number leaves out:** the two hours are the upper end of the therapists’ own self-reported time to write a session report from memory before LIAM, not the typical session; the 25 minutes are their review-and-submit time with LIAM’s draft in place, read by the team one quarter after rollout. I had left Genial Care by then: I designed and shipped LIAM, and the 25-minute figure is what the clinical team reported back. It is not a like-for-like total: narrating during the session adds a few minutes that the 25 does not include, and the population is the clinical team on staff, so this is a before-and-after with everyone, not a sample. The clinical lead’s verdict after launch was that record quality improved rather than merely held: a record written minutes after the session carries detail that one written from memory at 9pm does not.

The pressure on an AI feature is always to make it do more. The constraint I held was that LIAM proposes and never submits, even when the draft is good enough that signing it unread would be tempting. It cost us the most impressive version of the demo. It’s the reason the clinical side allowed the feature to exist at all.

**06** · What I’d do differently

## What I’d do differently

I would have brought the clinical lead into the interface decisions, not only the review of the output: several trust states would have been simpler if the person who owns the clinical standard had been in the room while they were being drawn. And I under-designed the moment a therapist corrects a specific field. The feedback prompt asks about LIAM’s suggestions in general, but editing a field never asks what was wrong with it, so the most precise signal in the whole feature goes unrecorded.

## Where this sits in the bigger picture

LIAM shipped after the family-facing app had already gone from 8% to 62% daily use. Once families were actually engaging, the constraint moved to the other side of the platform: the therapists producing the content families were now relying on. Same instinct, different audience: find where a person is spending effort on something that isn't the actual work, and compress it into a decision they can make quickly.

## Questions this page doesn't answer?

How the model was chosen, how we handled clinical-language accuracy, how the rollout reached the whole clinical team and what the feedback prompt was built to catch: all of it is a 30-minute call away.

Case study · Enterprise logistics · B2B

# Pick & Pack: one order, three people, one screen each

Fast Shop sells two-hour delivery, and the process behind that promise ran on phone calls and spreadsheets. I designed the platform that replaced them for the store, the distribution centre and the driver at once, with the exceptions treated as first-class screens.

Role
Sole product designer

Team
PM · Eng teams · Fast Shop ops

Client
Fast Shop

Timeline
Sep 2024 – Feb 2026

Scope
80+ stores · 22,000+ SKUs · web

The short version

**Problem:** Checkout promised delivery in two hours. Behind it, nobody could tell where an order was without a phone call, and a failed delivery had no defined next step.

**What I did:** Designed Pick & Pack for three roles at once instead of one primary user, treated the exception states as first-class screens, and rolled it out store by store.

**Outcome:** The two-hour promise held across 80+ stores on more volume than the operation had ever handled; operators stopped keeping parallel spreadsheets; a class of failed deliveries that had no name got a status and a next step.

Enterprise SaaS 0→1 platform Logistics Systems design

In this case 7 min read

- Why it was hard

- Decision: three roles, not one primary user

- The store board

- What shipped: the screens

- Rollout, store by store

- Impact

- What I'd do differently

**01** · Why it was hard

## Two hours, promised before anyone in a store knows the order exists

Fast Shop runs 80+ stores, 22,000+ SKUs and around 2,500 orders a day. Checkout sells delivery in two hours before anyone in a store has seen the order, and before Pick & Pack that promise ran on phone calls, a courier app and spreadsheets. The operation couldn’t even produce an on-time figure.

The number worth moving was time-to-detect: how long it takes an operator to find out an order is in trouble. Before the platform, that was whenever someone happened to notice or chased them about it, and an SLA is only met if exceptions surface early enough to fix.

I spent time with store operators asking where an order actually stops and what happens when a delivery fails. The honest answer was a manual loop: cancel the ride in the courier app, request a new one, track the driver by hand. Two things couldn’t change: the carrier integrations and the fiscal documents every order carries.

**02** · Decision: three roles, not one primary user

### One platform, three homes, one order

**Problem:** “Design it for the store operator and the rest will adapt” was a perfectly reasonable default. Most fulfilment tools pick one job and make the other two adapt to it.

**Decision:** Design for three jobs at once. A store sees its own queue, the distribution centre sees every store plus where the day is going wrong, the driver gets one unambiguous stop. Same order, same statuses, same colours, different first screen.

**Why:** The store needs to clear the queue before the courier arrives, the distribution centre needs to route around what’s about to breach, and the driver needs one clear next stop. Holding all three decided what goes first on a card and what earns an alert.

**Result:** One platform shipped with a different home per role, and no store, distribution centre or driver had to translate someone else's workflow into their own.

**03** · The store board

## The store board, shaped by the first delivery round

After the first round of deliveries, store operators came back with two requests. “I need to see the invoice number on the card, fast, to move my process along”: the fiscal invoice was what they looked up most, so it moved onto the card. “I need the most-late orders at the top, shouting on the screen, so I know what to prioritise”: lateness became the sort order and the loudest thing on the card, with time in status in red at the top, the remaining SLA on the pill and the carrier logo last.

[Image: Pick & Pack store board: four columns (order received, picking, ready for pickup, in transit) with order cards showing late flags, status pills with the remaining SLA, and the carrier logo]

- **1**“Late in this status” is the first thing on the card, in red, because it is the first question an operator asks.

- **2**Two pills, two questions: what is happening to the order, and how much of the promise is left (UltraFast · 1h).

- **3**The carrier logo sits last. You only need it once you have decided to act.

- **4**Columns follow the store’s own steps: received, picking, ready for pickup, in transit.

- **5**Click & Collect orders live on the same board with their own pill (“Retira”), so a store never runs two tools.

The store board as shipped.

**04** · What shipped: the screens

## What shipped: the screens

Below, the store and distribution-centre homes and the exceptions they share. The driver’s side is one stop at a time, and I walk through it on a call.

### The distribution centre: every store, and the numbers that say where the day is going wrong

The distribution centre sees every store at once, so its first screen is four counters (late, invoicing, transport, proof pending), each one a filter. Several operators work the same queue here, so every card shows who owns it.

[Image: Pick & Pack distribution-centre board with counters for late, invoicing, transport and proof-of-delivery problems across the top, cards showing who each order is allocated to, and a menu to unallocate or allocate to another user]

- **1**Four counters, each a filter: late, invoicing, transport, proof pending.

- **2**Allocation on the card: take an order off someone or hand it over in two clicks.

- **3**“Allocated to” on every card, so “is anyone on this?” stops being a shout across the floor.

- **4**Someone else’s card fades back: visible, not grabbable.

The distribution-centre board: the store’s cards plus ownership.

### The same queue as a table, when the question changes

Every hour the distribution centre asks which of 104 orders has waited longest, a question a board can’t answer. So the same queue toggles into a sortable table, with time in queue as its own column.

[Image: Pick & Pack distribution-centre table view: one row per order with a severity dot, store, modality, stage, status pill, carrier, creation time and time in queue, sortable by any column]

The same queue as a sortable table, for “what has waited longest.”

### When an order becomes a phone call

Whoever answers a customer call needs the whole story in seconds: the SLA countdown first, the history in order, and comments with attachments on the order itself instead of in someone’s head.

[Image: Pick & Pack order detail page: SLA countdown in red, time in current status flagged as late, customer and delivery data, order summary with products, a status history timeline and a comment thread with an attachment]

The order page, for the moment a delivery turns into a phone call.

### The exceptions are the product

In logistics, the exceptions decide whether an operator trusts the screen or works around it. Each of these four replaced something that used to be a phone call.

[Image: Modal for an order ready for pickup, flagged late: driver name, ID and plate, and a state saying the ride has not started with a tracking link]

The driver took the package and the ride never started Who has it, what car, a plain sentence saying the ride hasn’t begun, and tracking one click away. Used to be a call to the carrier.

[Image: Modal for a delivered order awaiting proof of delivery: a file upload area accepting images and documents, an uploaded screenshot, and a Complete order button]

Delivered, but not closed until there is proof An order closes when a photo or signature is attached, not when the driver says so. That is why “proof pending” is a counter on the distribution-centre home.

[Image: Modal for a click-and-collect order awaiting pickup: a QR code the customer scans to open a form with their data and a signature before taking the order]

Someone is at the counter to collect A QR code opens a form with the buyer’s data and signature, so the right person gets the product and the store keeps the record without a printer.

[Image: Export dialog for an order report with a warning that no orders were selected so all 104 will be exported, a name field and a Generating button]

Someone still needs a spreadsheet Exports stayed, with one guardrail: with nothing selected, the dialog says all 104 orders are about to be exported. Parallel spreadsheets falling out of use became our adoption signal.

Four of the 15 statuses in the shipped platform: the ones that replaced the most phone calls.

**05** · Rollout, store by store

## The release wasn't a date. It was a sequence

The flagship store went first, alone, watched daily until a full week passed without a new corner case. Then waves of about twenty stores every two weeks, close enough that problems were watched instead of reported. Three months of rollout and daily hypercare, then occasional tickets.

Each wave surfaced cases the first version didn’t handle, and each became a state or a rule. “Returning to store” is the one I’d point to. When a driver couldn’t deliver, the operator had to cancel the ride in the Uber app, request a new one to bring the package back and track the driver in the app by hand. We built that return into the platform: when a delivery fails, the trip back is created automatically and the operator follows it on the panel.

**06** · Impact

## The operation didn’t slow down. Even as the load went up

Three months after rollout, the platform was running the two-hour promise across 80+ stores on more volume than the operation had ever handled. Operators stopped keeping parallel spreadsheets, and a failed delivery went from invisible to a status with a next step.

80+ stores
Rolled out in waves over three months, running the two-hour promise on top of Fast Shop’s existing 22,000+ SKU catalogue

Chased → flagged
Time to detect an at-risk order: before, whenever someone happened to notice; after, the moment it enters “Late”

Statuses in the shipped taxonomy, four of them exceptions that replaced phone calls

**How it was measured:** the operation never produced an on-time figure before the platform, so there is no verified baseline, and I don’t present an estimate as one. Causality isn’t proven either: Fast Shop changed processes in the same months. The staged rollout, stores on the platform next to stores not yet on it, is the closest thing to a control.

**07** · What I'd do differently

## I shipped the first card without asking what operators look up first

The two changes that made the store board work, the invoice number on the card and the most-late orders on top, came from operators after the first delivery round. An afternoon watching a store counter before shipping would have surfaced both. I would also have captured time-to-detect from the first release, so this page could show a measured before-and-after.

### My role

The only designer on the platform, Sep 2024 to Feb 2026, across Pick & Pack, Compass, PIM and DevTools. Pick & Pack came first because it carried the two-hour promise.

### The team, and what was mine

A product manager owned the roadmap and OKRs with Fast Shop, Fast Shop’s operations leads were the domain experts, and one engineering team per product built it with me through every wave. Mine: three roles instead of a primary user, the store board and card, the table toggle, the four exception states and “returning to store.”

### Compass: the system underneath

A status pill means the same thing on the board, the table and the order page because the token layer underneath says so. That work became its own case.

Read the Compass case →

## Questions this page doesn't answer?

The research, the driver’s screen, how the rollout waves were sequenced and how we prioritised against Fast Shop’s OKRs: all of it is a 30-minute call away.

URL: https://cannalongadesign.github.io/compass/

Case study · Design Systems · Enterprise platform

# Compass: from one-off screens to a system three teams could build on

Before Compass, every screen at Kruzer was rebuilt from zero and nothing quite agreed with anything else. Building the system, and the semantic token scale underneath it, cut the cycle time on a design ticket from 4.2 to 2.5 days, measured in Jira.

Role
Senior Product Designer

Team
PM · Eng teams · Design

Client
Kruzer · Fast Shop

Timeline
Sep 2024 – Feb 2026

Outcome
4.2d → 2.5d cycle time, measured in Jira

The short version

**Problem:** Every screen started from an empty frame, so the same component was redrawn with small differences nobody had decided on.

**What I did:** Built the system from scratch: an audit with real counts, a three-layer semantic token scale where only the middle layer is allowed in design files, then migration and governance rules.

**Outcome:** Design-ticket cycle time dropped from **4.2 to 2.5 days**, measured in the Jira the engineering team already used.

Design systems Design tokens Platform design Governance

In this case 7 min read

- Why it was hard

- Decision: only the semantic layer ships

- Decision: governance is part of the deliverable

- What shipped

- Impact

- What I'd do differently

Compass is the design system I built from scratch at Kruzer, the platform behind Fast Shop's fulfillment operation. It started as a way to stop rebuilding the same status pill for the third time, and ended up as the layer that let three products stay coherent while the platform scaled to 80+ stores.

**01** · Why it was hard

## Before: everything took longer than it should

There was no shared foundation. Every new screen started from an empty frame, so the same components were redrawn over and over with small differences nobody had decided on: the primary button was one shade of blue in the queue and another in the order detail. Design took longer because nothing could be reused, engineering took longer because every handoff described a slightly new component, and review cycles took longer because most comments were about inconsistencies, not whether the solution was right.

No one funds tidiness, so the pointer I argued for was delivery speed: how long a change takes to get from decision to production, across three products on the same platform. That framing can be proven wrong (if cycle time didn’t move, Compass was an expensive preference), and tying it to a number engineering already tracked meant I was accountable to their measurement, not my own.

A design system that designers love and engineers route around is a failed one, so the founding conversation was with the people who would consume it: who owns a component once it exists, what a handoff needs to contain to stop being re-negotiated, and who is allowed to say no to a new variant. Settling those before the library had anything in it was the only moment that conversation was cheap.

“Consistency” is not a business case. Delivery speed is, and it can be proven wrong.

**02** · Decision: only the semantic layer ships

### Only the semantic layer is allowed in a design file

**Problem:** Naming tokens after what they look like (blue-500) tells you nothing about when to use them. People guess, and the guessing is where inconsistency comes back in.

**Decision:** Split three layers. Primitive: raw values like blue-500, space-4, referenced but never designed with directly. Semantic: what a value means (action-primary, status-success), the only layer a designer or engineer touches. Component: rare, purpose-built overrides.

**Why:** Asking “what breaks if we rebrand, or add dark mode” early is what forced the token layer to exist before the components. A system that can’t survive a colour change was never a system.

**Result:** Changing the meaning of “success” across three products became one edit. Adding a density mode became a token set. A new designer can read a file and understand why a colour is there.

**03** · Decision: governance is part of the deliverable

### A library without governance is just a folder

**Problem:** The part teams skip is the part that decides whether the system is alive in a year. A component nobody owns rots; a library with no rule against “just one more variant” drifts back into a folder.

**Decision:** Ship rules with the files, not after them: a new component has to prove it appears in at least two products, a change to a semantic token goes through review because it moves everything downstream, and anything deprecated gets a removal date instead of sitting there forever. Documentation counts as part of the component: a “use this when” that doesn’t exist is a component that will be misused.

**Why:** I asked engineers what they were actually missing when a spec arrived, and the answers shaped the documentation more than any design-system article did.

**Result:** Componentisation is where the rules stop being a document and start being enforced. A button is one component with variants for hierarchy, size, state and icon, spaced by token, not by hand: an engineer opening it receives a rule.

**04** · What shipped

## The user here is the team, and the job is confidence

Compass has no end user. Its users are designers and engineers, and what they need from it is the ability to make a decision once and not argue it again. Framed that way, the measure of success stops being how many components exist and becomes how few decisions each screen requires.

Compass · token playground

Accent

Radius 10px

Density

Order #48213
In transit

Distribution center · SLA 1h 42m remaining

Order #48219
Returning to store

Failed delivery · needs a next step

A live slice of Compass. Every component here reads from the same three tokens, so changing one keeps the whole set coherent.

[Image: Compass semantic token tables: each token named for its meaning, with the primitive value it resolves to]

The semantic layer, and the only one published to design files. $typography.h1.medium carries intent; 60px carries appearance. A designer who reaches for the second one is guessing, and the guessing is where inconsistency comes back in.

The component engineering questioned hardest was the data table. These products carry huge volumes of data, so advanced filters and user-customisable columns were a constant challenge, and the first versions didn’t serve every product. Getting to the right model took benchmarking against mature data-heavy products and testing several component variants until one worked for all three.

Composition is where the atom-and-molecule distinction stops being vocabulary. A select is not one component; it is a field, a label, a tooltip, a chip, a list and an error state composed together. Getting the composition right is what made a new select variant cost minutes instead of an afternoon.

[Image: The Compass select documentation: multi-select variants composed from field, label, tooltip, chips, list and error state]

Molecules: the select composed from smaller pieces: field, label, tooltip, chip, list, error. Composing instead of redrawing is what makes a new variant cost minutes.

**05** · Impact

## What it changed

There's no usability test for a design system, and no funnel: the evidence came from three places instead. The audit gave a hard before: around twenty blues, seven paddings and four button heights live in production, counted rather than estimated. Pick & Pack was the first consumer, proving the system against a real product before anyone else adopted it. And Jira, which the team already used to track demand, gave the after: the same class of work, measured before and after adoption. A metric I invent to prove my own project is worth roughly nothing in a review; a metric engineering already trusts is much harder to wave away.

The clearest signal came from the tracker: once teams were building from Compass instead of from scratch, Jira throughput on design demands rose by about 40%, and review comments shifted from spacing and colour to whether the flow was right. What that number can't prove, and I'd say so before anyone asked: ticket throughput is confounded (the team also grew and the sprint cadence changed once), so the 40% is the delta engineering leads read from their own board over the same class of work, the best number available, not a controlled one. The review-comment shift is the softer signal, and honestly the one I trust more, because nobody can game what a colleague chooses to argue about.

4.2d → 2.5d
Cycle time on the same class of design ticket, before and after adoption: the harder number, found late

40%
Design-ticket throughput in Jira after adoption, same class of work; a tracker delta, not a controlled experiment

Products on one shared foundation

~20
Near-identical blues counted live in production before the audit, the baseline that turned a feeling into a number

**How it was measured:** both numbers come from the Jira board engineering already used to track demand, comparing the same class of design ticket before and after adoption: 40% on throughput, 4.2 days down to 2.5 on cycle time. Neither is a controlled experiment, and both are readings I recall rather than a report I can still pull. The measurement had to belong to someone other than me, or it would have been marketing; the confounds above are named on purpose.

**06** · What I'd do differently

### What I’d do differently

I would have led with a different number. Throughput was the easy metric to reach for; cycle time, roughly 4.2 days down to 2.5, is the harder one to argue with, and I only went looking for it after 40% was already the headline.

## What I'd defend in a design review

The decision I would defend hardest is refusing to let the component layer grow. Every one-off override was a signal that the semantic layer had a gap, and fixing the gap is slower in the moment and cheaper for everyone after. I also count governance as part of the deliverable: a system nobody owns drifts back to where it started.

The argument I had to win was with engineering, because a system is adopted by people who didn't ask for it, and this one was about taking something away: only the semantic layer would be published, meaning giving up a naming convention they were comfortable with. What made it land was the audit: twenty near-identical blues live in production is not an opinion, and it moved the conversation from taste to cost in one meeting.

## Questions this page doesn't answer?

The token naming decisions, the audit that started it, how long Compass took and what it displaced, and how I handled the components teams did not want to give up: all of it is a 30-minute call away.

Case study · Consumer trust · AI product

# Safe Site Detector: from more data to a decision people can act on

Reclame AQUI’s site detector had to be rebuilt in-house, fast. I led design for the AI-powered replacement and reframed it around one question: does the person understand the result well enough to decide whether to buy?

Role

Senior Product Designer

Team

PM · Head of Product · Engineering

Company

Reclame AQUI

Timeline

Jun 2026 – ongoing

Outcome

Decision rate 45.1% → 72.4% · cost R$1.7M → R$1.2k a month

In this case 7 min read

Why it was hard

An experiment in six weeks

Decision: test comprehension

Decision: a verdict built on evidence

Designing for AI readers

Impact

What I’d do differently

The short version

Problem:

The partner behind the site detector would start charging per query: R$1.7M a month at our volume. The detector had no way to show whether it helped anyone decide, and a yes-or-no verdict about a company is a heavy claim to make on a public page.

What I did:

Owned data discovery and design end to end: an AI-first experiment live in about six weeks, a comprehension test inside the product, a V2 whose verdict is built on protection shields and worded to state only what was verified, and a staged rollout to 100% of users, three months from first conversation to full launch.

Outcome:

The share of people who said the detector helped them decide went from **45.1% to 72.4%**, and in the comprehension test the refined version was read correctly by **74% of people, against 29%**. The rebuild also took the projected cost from R$1.7M to R$1.2k a month. V2 is live for everyone on Reclame AQUI’s own engine.

AI product design Trust & safety In-product research LLM-ready content

[Image: Safe Site Detector home page on a desktop monitor: paste a link and check whether a site is trustworthy]

The detector’s public home page. Everything below is told through the process and illustrations, not internal screens.

### Try the detector live

It’s public and free: paste any store’s address and see the shields.

Open the detector →

**01** · Why it was hard

## A trust product that had to be rebuilt without losing trust

Reclame AQUI is where Brazilian shoppers check a company’s reputation before buying, the closest local equivalent to Trustpilot. Its site detector tells people whether a store’s website looks safe. It ran on a partner’s engine, and when the partnership ended the partner would start charging about R$10 per query: R$1.7M a month at our volume.

Speed was one constraint. The other was the nature of the answer. A detector that labels a company’s site as unreliable is making a strong public statement about that company, and the old product had no measure of whether its answers helped anyone decide.

So I framed the work the way the business needed it, and held every decision below to it:

- **Outcome** Retire the partner’s detector before its per-query price turned into R$1.7M a month. That was the main pain, and the deadline.

- **Job to be done** “Is this site a scam or not, before I pay?” The screen had one job, and everything on it had to serve that answer.

- **Who it had to work for** Dona Neide, an older woman in a small town in Acre, deep in Brazil’s interior, checking whether the store selling the skirt she wants is safe. If it was simple and clear for her, it was simple and clear for everyone.

- **Opportunity** The rebuild was forced by cost, so we used it to clear the debt the page carried: accessibility, a visual identity that did not follow the design system, and technical debt along the way.

**02** · An experiment in six weeks

## Live in about six weeks, measured from the start

To move fast, engineering built the first version AI-first: a crawler collects public signals about the site and the company behind it, and a model writes the analysis from four of them:

- **Site security** the technical security of the site itself.

- **Phishing alerts** whether the address appears in phishing alerts.

- **Company** public information about who runs it.

- **Domain** domain data, such as how long it has existed.

Before launch, I ran a short design critique to cut cognitive load and scroll. The experiment then replaced the partner’s detector for about a month, with the decision metric Reclame AQUI uses across its products attached: a question inside the product that asks whether the information helped the person decide whether to buy. For the first time the detector had a success metric, and a baseline: a **45.1% decision rate**.

### More data, harder decisions

The experiment collected far more information than before, but it never said what it concluded. Every signal was left for the user to interpret, so a tool built to help people decide handed the decision back to them. The design problem became helping people understand the conclusion quickly, and why the system reached it.

**03** · Decision: test comprehension 1

### Test whether people read the result correctly

Problem

The easy question was “how do we lay this out?” A preference test would have picked the nicest screen and said nothing about whether people understood it.

Decision

I reframed the work around the user’s job on this screen and tested performance: does the person read the verdict correctly, and act in line with it? In Useberry, each person saw one version: the experiment, or a refined version I designed from the critique. Getting the verdict right, acting on it and effort decided the winner.

Why

A heatmap of the previous page showed attention almost entirely on the link field and the analyse button, and a benchmark of public tools like ScamAdviser and ScamDoc showed how others structure a safety result. Both showed where people look. Neither showed whether they understood what they saw, which is what a trust product depends on.

What it caught

Faced with a site that was safe, 46% of people using the experiment chose “be careful” and 25% “I don’t know”. Its extra data was making a safe site look doubtful.

Result

The refined version was read correctly by 74% of people, against 29% for the experiment, and it became the base for V2.

74% vs 29%

Read a safe site correctly as safe: refined version vs the experiment

52% vs 21%

Would buy from that safe site

6% vs 21%

Would avoid buying from it

**How to read it:** 55 answers from 450 visits, so the gap is large and directional, not a population number.

### What the interviews added

People who finished the test could volunteer for an interview. The script never put screens side by side, so it measured the screen rather than my explanation of it. Four findings:

- **Reputation decides; the shields support it.** The analysis matters most where a company has no reputation yet.

- **The verification seal didn’t explain itself.** People described it through outside references, like a social network’s verified badge.

- **Trust and reputation only separated on a closer read.** At first glance, a mixed result looked contradictory.

- **Shield colours confused people.** They expected a traffic light.

Findings went back into critiques, and a MaxDiff ranked which questions about a company deserve space on the page. Each finding became a direction for V2: the verdict before the detail, the site being analysed at the top, a seal that explains itself, and traffic-light colours.

**04** · Decision: a verdict built on evidence 2

### A clear verdict, worded to state only what was verified

Problem

Shoppers need a clear answer, but a wrong claim about a company can harm a legitimate business and give it grounds to sue. Showing raw data avoids the claim and leaves all the interpretation to the user.

Decision

Every analysis ends in a verdict, from 0 to 5 shields, and each shield shows the signal behind it. The copy states as fact only what the analysis can prove: a site is called a scam only when we confirm it is stealing people’s data. Everything else is described as what we found, so the message lands without claiming more than the evidence supports.

Why

The shields make the verdict easy to read and easy to check: people see the conclusion and the reason for it in seconds, and the company can see exactly which signal shaped the result. Every word was reviewed with that legal weight in mind.

Result

V2 kept the depth of the analysis and gave people a verdict they can act on, with every statement on the screen backed by what was verified.

Before: every signal, no conclusion

After: the verdict first, evidence below

Abstract wireframes of the idea, not the product screens.

### Five shields

- **Brand imitation** whether the address tries to pass as a known brand, or shows signs of data theft.

- **Site security** the site’s certificate and technical structure.

- **Company identity** whether the company exists and its tax registration is active.

- **Consumer behaviour** unrealistic offers, false urgency and suspicious contacts.

- **Reputation and seal** the company’s reputation on Reclame AQUI and its verification seal.

### Six levels, one report each

**Signs of imitation** 0/5

**High risk** 1/5

**Low trust** 2/5

**Partial trust** 3/5

**Probably trustworthy** 4/5

**Trustworthy** 5/5

Every analysis lands on one of six levels, from 0 to 5 shields, each with its own report: what was checked, which shield the site didn’t pass, and what to do next. While the analysis runs, the screen shows each source being checked. When a site can’t be reached, an error says so and offers a retry.

**05** · Designing for AI readers

## A second reader: the AI answering for the shopper

More and more people ask an AI assistant whether a store is trustworthy before they open any website. Engineering structured the detector’s data with JSON-LD, and I revised the interface to support it. Models favour question-and-answer content, so the page now opens with the question people actually ask, whether the site is trustworthy, and answers four short ones first: is it trustworthy, does the company exist, what is its reputation, does it have the seal.

Across 30 companies, citations in Google AI Overview rose 138%, measured in Search Console. The same screen now serves two readers: the person deciding on a purchase, and the assistant answering on their behalf.

**06** · Impact

## Cheaper, live, and easier to decide with

- 01 Experiment

- 02 Critique

- 03 Comprehension test

- 04 Interviews

- 05 V2

- 06 Rollout 20%

- 07 50%

- 08 100%

From first conversation to full launch in three months. An illustration of the process, not the product.

V2, the version that came out of the research, went live in stages: 20% of users, then 50%, then 100% in September 2026. At each step we watched for errors and user reports and adjusted before widening, so a wrong answer about a company would reach as few people as possible. It now runs for everyone on Reclame AQUI’s own engine.

45.1% → 72.4%

People who said the detector helped them decide, experiment vs V2

-99.9%

Monthly cost, from a projected R$1.7M to R$1.2k for 171.7k analyses

MetricBeforeV2Change Monthly costR$1.7M (projected)R$1.2k for 171.7k analyses-99.9%Cost per analysisR$10under R$0.01-99.9%Decision rate45.1% (experiment)72.4%+27.3 pp

Three things changed:

- **It answers the question people came with.** The verdict comes first, and the shields explain it.

- **It is fair to the company being analysed.** The verdict states only what the analysis can prove, and each shield shows the signal behind it.

- **It can be measured.** The decision metric gives the team a running read on whether the detector helps people decide, which the old product never had.

The feedback loop is still running. Since reaching 100%, the back-end rules and the way the AI behaves have evolved considerably. When a corner case appears, we investigate whether the cause is ours or a configuration in that company’s own Reclame AQUI profile that is affecting the detector’s answer, and fix it at the right end.

**How it was measured:** the R$1.7M is the partner’s per-query price applied to our volume, not an invoice we paid; the R$1.2k is V2’s actual monthly cost for 171.7k analyses. Both decision rates come from the same in-product decision question, read during the experiment and after V2: a before-and-after, not a controlled test. The +138% compares Google AI Overview citations in Search Console for the 30 companies in the experiment.

**07** · What I’d do differently

## Hold the screen to its job, and align earlier

Most of what I would change is about focus and alignment, not the screen itself.

- **Hold every version to the job from day one.** The crawler could gather far more than the screen needed, and even the refined versions kept wanting to show more. It took several design rounds to cut back to what answered “is this a scam?”. I would make the job the filter for every piece of information from the first sketch, to keep cognitive load low from the start.

- **Bring every decision level, and the neighbouring teams, in at the start.** Decisions passed through several levels, and a direction approved at one could meet new context at the next and come back for rework. The detector also touches journeys other teams own, from B2C to B2B to the logged-in area. I would put the people who shape the decision together earlier, so context arrives before the design, not after it.

- **Ask the three-sided question first.** Every decision has to be good for Reclame AQUI, for the company being analysed and for the consumer. If one of the three is left unprotected, the idea usually needs rethinking, and asking it at the start avoids rework later.

I would also look at the data companies send about themselves before designing the answer: a detector is only as good as what goes into it. It was my first time designing inside a market leader of this size, where many teams and decision levels shape one journey. Learning to work across those layers, and to adapt when the context changed, is what I take into the next project.

### The team, and what was mine

A PM and the Head of Product owned scope and priorities, and engineering built the experiment, the analysis pipeline and the structured data. Mine: data discovery, the design critique, the research plan and comprehension test, the refined version, the shield structure and how each level is explained, and the interface changes for AI readers.

## Questions this page doesn't answer?

The rules behind each shield, how the test was built and how each number was measured: all of it is a 30-minute call away.
